Revisiting AdaGrad in Stochastic Convex Optimization: Last Iterates, High Probability, and Lower Bounds

Weiming Ou Note: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, email: ouweiming@163.sufe.edu.cn    Xiao Wang Note: MoE Key Laboratory of Interdisciplinary Research of Computation and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, email: wangxiao@sufe.edu.cn
Abstract

AdaGrad and AdaGrad-Norm are widely used adaptive methods, but their precise behavior in stochastic convex optimization remains less understood. We first show that AdaGrad-Norm and AdaGrad do not admit any universal last-iterate rate, even under sub-Gaussian noise and bounded iterates. We then prove that bounded variance alone is too weak: even with bounded iterates, it cannot yield high-probability average-iterate rates, and without bounded iterates it may not even guarantee convergence in expectation. Besides, we construct tight Ω⁡(log⁡T/T)\Omega(\log T/\sqrt{T}) lower bounds for both AdaGrad-Norm and AdaGrad under sub-Gaussian noise, showing that log⁡T\log T in existing average-iterate upper bounds is unavoidable. Finally, we show that this log⁡T\log T loss disappears once bounded-iterate condition is imposed: under a general ABC condition, both methods achieve rates O⁡(1/T){O}(1/\sqrt{T}).

1 Introduction

AdaGrad scales its updates using the gradients observed so far, replacing a prescribed stepsize schedule by a data-dependent normalization. The original coordinate-wise method was developed in online convex optimization by McMahan and Streeter [32] and Duchi et al. [8]. AdaGrad-Norm instead uses a single accumulator for the cumulative squared gradient norms [45]. Although the methods share a common regret-analysis framework, their stochastic guarantees depend on the noise model, the output, and the behavior of the iterates.

For smooth convex objectives, average-iterate bounds are available for delayed AdaGrad-type schemes [24], standard AdaGrad-Norm under suitable tail assumptions [3, 29], and coordinate-wise AdaGrad on bounded domains [28]. Log-free, noise-adaptive rates also have precedents on bounded domains or under bounded-iterate assumptions [22, 43]. These guarantees do not automatically describe the final point returned by an implementation. Our central question is therefore whether the standard updates admit an explicit, vanishing last-iterate rate under the same smoothness, light-tail, and stability conditions.

Our main result gives a negative answer in the general conditional-oracle model. For every proposed positive sequence rT→0r_{T}\to 0, we construct one smooth convex objective and one infinite-horizon, conditionally unbiased sub-Gaussian oracle such that the expected last-iterate error exceeds rTr_{T} by an unbounded factor along a deterministic subsequence. All iterates remain inside an arbitrarily prescribed radius. Thus the issue is not merely a missing polynomial exponent: no prescribed vanishing rate is valid uniformly over this class. The hard instance itself converges, separating convergence from a uniform quantitative guarantee. Its oracle is time- and history-dependent, so the result does not preclude rates under additional sampling restrictions.

A second question concerns the confidence of an averaged output. Averaging often gives guarantees unavailable for the last iterate, but we show that it does not repair the poor confidence dependence of unmodified AdaGrad under finite variance. Our construction combines three properties: a fixed infinite-horizon instance, the uniformly averaged iterate, and any prescribed almost-sure trajectory radius. This output distinction matters: the lower bound in Chezhegov et al. [5, Theorem B.4], specialized to zero momentum, is stated for the last iterate. A last-iterate lower bound alone does not establish an average-iterate lower bound. Our result excludes polynomial decay in time with only polylogarithmic dependence on the inverse failure probability.

The remaining results place these two limitations in context. Without a common stability radius, finite variance permits constant worst-case expected average error. Even under bounded, hence sub-Gaussian, noise, a scalar construction gives an Ω⁡(log⁡T/T)\Omega(\log T/\sqrt{T}) average-error lower bound for the fixed-parameter unprojected updates and a corresponding inverse-square-root SGD schedule. With bounded iterates, by contrast, classical regret analysis yields explicit noise-adaptive average-error bounds under the conditional ABC model. The distinction between a fixed instance and a horizon-dependent family is kept explicit throughout: choosing a different function for each horizon does not establish nonconvergence on one fixed instance.

1.1 Our contributions

Table 1 summarizes the results in the order developed below. Every lower-bound construction is one-dimensional and applies to both AdaGrad-Norm and coordinate-wise AdaGrad.

  1. 1.

    No universal vanishing last-iterate rate. Theorem 3.1 shows that every prescribed rT→0r_{T}\to 0 is violated by a single fixed sub-Gaussian instance with bounded iterates. Its expected error satisfies 𝔼⁡[ΔTn]/rTn→∞\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{T_{n}}]/r_{T_{n}}\to\infty along a deterministic subsequence. Delayed bounded pulses keep the accumulator small until an arbitrarily late time; the resulting displacement defeats the proposed rate without preventing convergence of the constructed instance.

  2. 2.

    A high-probability limitation for the average iterate. Theorem 3.5 excludes polynomial-in-TT rates with only polynomial dependence on log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta) for uniform averaging, on one fixed infinite-horizon finite-variance instance inside any prescribed radius D>0D>0. A pulse cascade increases the accumulator through alternating small displacements. The combination of fixed-instance quantifiers, averaged output, and arbitrary stability radius distinguishes the statement from the last-iterate lower bound of Chezhegov et al. [5]; the general heavy-tail difficulty itself is already known.

  3. 3.

    Average-error lower bounds without a uniform stability radius. Theorem 3.8 gives a horizon-dependent family with constant worst-case expected average error under independent identically distributed additive finite-variance noise. Theorem 3.10 gives Ω⁡(η​σ​log⁡T/T)\Omega(\eta\sigma\log T/\sqrt{T}) under sub-Gaussian noise, even from a minimizer. Both concern fixed algorithm parameters. The latter construction also proves a smooth-convex average-error lower bound for inverse-square-root SGD; the final part of Appendix D shows that its SGD version can use independent bounded additive noise.

  4. 4.

    An explicit noise-adaptive ABC upper bound. Under bounded iterates, Theorem 3.14 gives O⁡(T−1+C/T)O(T^{-1}+\sqrt{C/T}) expected average error, with initialization and the ABC coefficients explicit. The C=0C=0 case gives O⁡(T−1)O(T^{-1}) even with state-dependent noise. This is a unified extension of classical regret and self-bounding analysis [8, 22, 43], not a new noise-adaptation principle. It assumes, rather than proves, trajectory stability.

1.2 Related work

Last-iterate convergence versus uniform rates.

Last-iterate convergence has been studied extensively for stochastic gradient methods [4, 48, 42, 36, 37, 26], stochastic mirror descent [31], and momentum methods based on follow-the-regularized-leader updates [23]. For adaptive methods, Li and Orabona [24] analyze delayed updates, while Jin et al. [19], Jin and Wang [18] study qualitative stochastic convergence of current-gradient AdaGrad under their respective assumptions. The deterministic nonsmooth analysis of Preobrazhenskaia et al. [38] concerns another setting. Theorem 3.1 does not assert a first qualitative convergence theorem. It instead rules out every prescribed uniform vanishing rate under smoothness, bounded iterates, and a general conditional sub-Gaussian oracle. The distinction is substantive: almost-sure convergence of individual trajectories does not supply a uniform expected rate for the entire oracle class.

High-probability guarantees and the averaged output.

Foundational and subsequent high-probability analyses of stochastic mirror descent and gradient methods include Nemirovski et al. [34], Gorbunov et al. [12], Gorbunov et al. [13], Li and Orabona [25]. Clipping can control heavy-tailed gradients [6, 27]; high-probability analyses for adaptive methods include Kavis et al. [20], Attia and Koren [3], Hong and Lin [16], Hong and Lin [15]. Most directly, Chezhegov et al. [5] establish poor confidence dependence for unmodified adaptive methods and show how clipping improves it. Their Theorem B.4 concerns the event f⁡(xK)−f⁡(x⋆)≥εf(x_{K})-f(x^{\star})\geq\varepsilon for the last iterate of their momentum-AdaGrad update; setting the momentum coefficient to zero recovers AdaGrad-Norm. Our Theorem 3.5 directly controls f⁡(x¯T)−f⁡(x⋆)f(\bar{x}_{T})-f(x^{\star}) instead, on one fixed infinite-horizon instance within an arbitrary prescribed radius. The proof keeps the post-cascade iterates on the same side of the minimizer, so averaging cannot cancel the long-lived displacement. This is an averaged-output obstruction, not an inference from a last-iterate event. It remains compatible with weaker confidence bounds obtained from expectation by Markov’s inequality.

Lower bounds for SGD and adaptive methods.

Classical oracle-complexity and information-theoretic results establish an Ω(T−1/2)\Omega(T^{-1/2}) stochastic term for suitable convex problem classes [35, 1, 39]. The logarithmic lower bound of Harvey et al. [14] concerns a nonsmooth last iterate; it does not give a smooth-convex lower bound for uniform averaging. Lower bounds for nonconvex stationarity [2, 17] and structured nonconvex objectives [41] concern different settings. Recent smooth-convex SGD analyses include last-iterate upper bounds [31, 11]. We are not aware of an earlier Ω⁡(log⁡T/T)\Omega(\log T/\sqrt{T}) lower bound for the exact combination considered here: uniformly averaged unprojected SGD, a smooth convex objective, bounded noise, and a fixed inverse-square-root stepsize schedule. Theorem 3.10 and its SGD extension in Appendix D establish this statement directly. This scoped comparison is not a lower bound for all SGD schedules: properly tuned finite-horizon steps and averaging admit different guarantees [34].

Adaptive methods and noise adaptation.

The online analysis of McMahan and Streeter [32], Duchi et al. [8] provides the starting point for adaptive normalization. Related developments include adaptive steplength rules and variants of AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam [47, 33, 40], delayed AdaGrad-type schemes [24], and standard updates under stronger tail assumptions [3, 29]. On a bounded convex set, Levy et al. [22] obtain a log-free O⁡(L​D2/T+σ​D/T)O(LD^{2}/T+\sigma D/\sqrt{T}) expected bound for scalar AdaGrad. Under bounded iterates and component-function assumptions, Vaswani et al. [43] derive an analogous noise-adaptive transition using regret, self-bounding, and a quadratic inequality. Their residual-noise parameter differs from the conditional variance bound used here. Coordinate-wise adaptation under anisotropic smoothness and noise is studied by Liu et al. [28]. Our Theorem 3.14 keeps constants explicit under the global conditional ABC model. A broader nonconvex literature studies scalar and coordinate-wise normalization [7, 20, 10, 9, 30, 46, 44, 16].

Oracle and filtration.

At xtx_{t}, the oracle returns gt=∇f​(xt)+ξtg_{t}=\nabla f(x_{t})+\xi_{t}. The initialization x1x_{1} is deterministic, ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is trivial, and ℱt=σ⁡(g1,…,gt)\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma(g_{1},\ldots,g_{t}), so xtx_{t} is ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable. Assumption 1.

For some L>0L>0, for all x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖≤L​‖x−y‖.\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|.

For some σ>0\sigma>0,

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(‖ξt‖2σ2)|ℱt−1]≤e.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{\|\xi_{t}\|^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right)\middle|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]\leq e.

For some σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, 𝔼⁡[‖ξt‖2∣ℱt−1]≤σ2\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_{t}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq\sigma^{2}.

There are A,B,C≥0A,B,C\geq 0 such that

𝔼⁡[‖gt‖2∣ℱt−1]≤A​Δt+B​‖∇f​(xt)‖2+C.\mathbb{E}[\|g_{t}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq A\Delta_{t}+B\|\nabla f(x_{t})\|^{2}+C. (2.1)
Remark 2.1.

Conditional Jensen’s inequality shows that Assumption 3 implies Assumption 4. Together with unbiasedness, bounded variance implies the ABC condition with (A,B,C)=(0,1,σ2)(A,B,C)=(0,1,\sigma^{2}). The ABC framework therefore includes both preceding noise models [21]. The case C=0C=0 permits state-dependent noise; it does not require every gradient to be deterministic.

For b0,η>0b_{0},\eta>0, AdaGrad-Norm uses

bt2=b02+∑s=1t‖gs‖2,xt+1=xt−η​gtbt.b_{t}^{2}=b_{0}^{2}+\sum_{s=1}^{t}\|g_{s}\|^{2},\qquad x_{t+1}=x_{t}-\eta\frac{g_{t}}{b_{t}}. (AdaGrad-Norm)

All lower bounds exploit this common scalar update, whereas the upper bound treats the two normalizations separately and allows arbitrary positive b0,ib_{0,i}.

3 Main results

We first rule out a universal last-iterate rate, then show that averaging does not remove the high-probability obstruction under finite variance. The next two results address expected average error without a common stability radius. The final theorem gives the complementary noise-adaptive upper bound when stability is available.

3.1 No universal vanishing last-iterate rate

Our first result concerns the expected error at the actual final iterate. Neither smoothness, sub-Gaussian noise, nor an arbitrarily small trajectory radius supplies a universal vanishing rate in the conditional-oracle model.

Theorem 3.1 (Arbitrarily slow last-iterate convergence).

Fix L,σ,b0,η,D>0L,\sigma,b_{0},\eta,D>0. For every prescribed sequence rT>0r_{T}>0 with rT→0r_{T}\to 0, there exist a single convex LL-smooth quadratic f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, a single infinite-horizon oracle satisfying Assumptions 2 and 3, and deterministic Tn→∞T_{n}\to\infty, such that both algorithms, initialized at x1=x⋆=0x_{1}=x^{\star}=0, satisfy |xt−x⋆|≤D|x_{t}-x^{\star}|\leq D almost surely for all t≥1t\geq 1 and

𝔼⁡[f⁡(xTn)−f⋆]rTn⟶∞.\frac{\mathbb{E}[f(x_{T_{n}})-f^{\star}]}{r_{T_{n}}}\longrightarrow\infty. (3.1)
Proof sketch.

At the minimizer of a small quadratic, both the iterate and accumulator stay unchanged until a nonzero pulse occurs. At scheduled times τn\tau_{n}, allow symmetric noise of fixed magnitude with probability q/(n+1)2q/(n+1)^{2}, and switch off all noise after the first pulse. That pulse creates a fixed displacement, followed by deterministic contraction. Its occurrence probability gives 𝔼⁡[Δτn+1]≥c1/(n+1)2\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{\tau_{n}+1}]\geq c_{1}/(n+1)^{2}; see (A.4). Choosing τn\tau_{n} so that rτn+1≤(n+1)−4r_{\tau_{n}+1}\leq(n+1)^{-4} proves the claim. The delay, rather than growing noise magnitude, defeats the rate. Appendix A also verifies asymptotic convergence of this particular instance. ∎

Remark 3.2.

The quantifiers select an instance after the proposed sequence rTr_{T}, but then hold it fixed for all evaluation times. Thus the theorem is stronger than excluding every polynomial exponent separately, and is not a horizon-by-horizon change of oracle. The quantifier is ∀(rT→0)​∃ℐ​∃(Tn)\forall(r_{T}\to 0)\,\exists\mathcal{I}\,\exists(T_{n}), not the existence of one instance slower than every possible sequence. The constructed instance satisfies 𝔼⁡[Δt]→0\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}]\to 0; no general qualitative convergence theorem is asserted. An explicit schedule, independent of a proposed rate, gives

𝔼⁡[ΔTn]≥c(1+log⁡log⁡Tn)2,Tn=⌈exp⁡(exp⁡n)⌉+1,\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{T_{n}}]\geq\frac{c}{(1+\log\log T_{n})^{2}},\qquad T_{n}=\lceil\exp(\exp n)\rceil+1, (3.2)

where c>0c>0 depends only on L,σ,b0,η,DL,\sigma,b_{0},\eta,D. The schedule for an arbitrary rTr_{T} need not be this particular one. The obstruction uses delayed, time- and history-dependent noise, not unbounded pulse magnitudes; it does not rule out rates under additional oracle restrictions.

Remark 3.3.

The construction uses a fixed objective and bounded pulses. The objective is a strongly convex quadratic with curvature ℓ=min⁡{L,b0/(2​η)}\ell=\min\{L,b_{0}/(2\eta)\}, independent of the proposed rate. Its minimizer, the initialization, the radius, and the pulse magnitude MM are also fixed independently of rTr_{T}. In fact, the construction satisfies the stronger pathwise bounds |ξt|≤M|\xi_{t}|\leq M and |gt|≤ℓ​d0+M|g_{t}|\leq\ell d_{0}+M, with d0≤Dd_{0}\leq D. Only the scheduled pulse times depend on rTr_{T}. Thus the obstruction is neither a flattening sequence of objectives nor increasingly large gradients. It arises because elapsed time need not force growth of the adaptive accumulator: the oracle can remain noiseless at a minimizer for an arbitrarily long interval. The uniform moment assumptions control pulse size and probability but do not impose a clock on when stochastic variation must occur.

Remark 3.4.

Averaging can still have a rate because it dilutes a late excursion: before the pulse, the objective error is zero and the accumulator stays at b0b_{0}; immediately afterward, the last iterate has a fixed error. A late evaluation can therefore detect the entire displacement, whereas uniform averaging dilutes a short late excursion by the horizon. This explains why Theorem 3.14 can give an explicit expected average-iterate rate on the same class. An average-iterate upper bound cannot be converted into a last-iterate rate merely by substituting the final point.

3.2 A high-probability limitation even for the average iterate

We next weaken the noise assumption to finite variance and ask for a high-probability guarantee for the uniform average, rather than the last iterate. The following result combines one fixed infinite-horizon instance, this averaged output, and any prescribed bounded-trajectory radius.

Theorem 3.5 (No polynomial average-iterate rate with polylogarithmic confidence).

Fix L,σ,b0,η,D>0L,\sigma,b_{0},\eta,D>0. There exist a fixed one-dimensional convex LL-smooth quadratic and a fixed infinite-horizon oracle satisfying Assumptions 2 and 4, such that both algorithms, initialized at x1=x⋆=0x_{1}=x^{\star}=0, satisfy |xt−x⋆|≤D|x_{t}-x^{\star}|\leq D almost surely for every t≥1t\geq 1. There also exist deterministic Tn→∞T_{n}\to\infty, δn∈(0,1/2)\delta_{n}\in(0,1/2), and constants c⋆,K>0c_{\star},K>0 such that

ℙ{f(x¯Tn)−f⋆≥c⋆}\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\{f(\bar{x}_{T_{n}})-f^{\star}\geq c_{\star}\} ≥2​δn,\displaystyle\geq 2\delta_{n}, (3.3)
log⁡(1/δn)\displaystyle\log(1/\delta_{n}) ≤K​(1+log⁡Tn)2.\displaystyle\leq K(1+\log T_{n})^{2}.

Consequently, no bound

f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆≤K0​[T−a+P⁡(log⁡(1/δ))​T−b],a,b>0,f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}\leq K_{0}\bigl[T^{-a}+P(\log(1/\delta))T^{-b}\bigr],\qquad a,b>0, (3.4)

can hold with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta for every T≥1T\geq 1 and δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2), with K0<∞K_{0}<\infty and a fixed polynomial PP, nonnegative on [log⁡2,∞)[\log 2,\infty), independent of T,δT,\delta.

Proof sketch.

A single large gradient can move the iterate almost η\eta, so it cannot respect an arbitrary radius D<ηD<\eta. Instead, arrange a finite random cascade whose designated path alternates between 00 and −d0-d_{0}, while the accumulator grows geometrically; see (B.2). Rare pulses preserve a common conditional variance bound, and every departure switches off the noise. Stopping after an odd number nn of pulses leaves a nonzero displacement and an exponentially large accumulator, so the displacement survives for an exponentially long horizon. The designated event has probability at least exp⁡(−O⁡(n2))\exp(-O(n^{2})), yielding (3.3). Appendix B checks all paths and the fixed-oracle quantifier. ∎

Remark 3.6.

Our result concerns the averaged output on one fixed bounded instance. The last-iterate event in Chezhegov et al. [5, Theorem B.4] does not by itself lower-bound f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}. Convexity gives an upper bound on f⁡(x¯T)f(\bar{x}_{T}) by the mean of the iterate values, not the lower bound needed here. Our cascade instead creates a displacement that persists for a substantial fraction of the horizon. On the designated event all iterates are nonpositive and the late ones have magnitude at least d0/2d_{0}/2, so their uniform average has magnitude at least d0/4d_{0}/4; see (B.8). The argument directly excludes the stated confidence dependence even for this more forgiving output.

The fixed-instance quantifier is particularly strong here. Once the cascade law has been chosen from L,σ,b0,η,DL,\sigma,b_{0},\eta,D, the same instance excludes every pair of positive exponents and every fixed polynomial appearing in (3.4). It is not retuned for a proposed confidence bound. Small oscillations consume normalization while leaving little net displacement; after the last designated pulse, the accumulated normalization prevents rapid recovery. This separates trajectory containment from concentration of the averaged objective error. In contrast, a single large initial pulse need not respect a prescribed radius smaller than η\eta.

Remark 3.7.

The obstruction concerns confidence dependence rather than nonconvergence: the levels δn\delta_{n} shrink with the horizons. The theorem does not say that the averaged error fails to vanish for a fixed δ\delta, nor that averaging fails almost surely on the hard instance. Indeed, Theorem 3.14 and Markov’s inequality give, in dimension one, for every δ>0\delta>0,

ℙ{f(x¯T)−f⋆>1δ(2​L​Γ2+Γ​b0T+Γ​σT)}≤δ,Γ=D22​η+η.\mathbb{P}\!\left\{f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}>\frac{1}{\delta}\left(\frac{2L\Gamma^{2}+\Gamma b_{0}}{T}+\frac{\Gamma\sigma}{\sqrt{T}}\right)\right\}\leq\delta,\quad\Gamma=\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}+\eta. (3.5)

Its 1/δ1/\delta dependence is outside the class excluded by (3.4). Thus the substantive distinction is that uniform averaging does not upgrade finite variance to a polynomial rate with polylogarithmic confidence dependence, even on one fixed bounded instance.

3.3 Finite variance permits constant worst-case average error

The previous theorem retains a bounded trajectory and isolates confidence dependence. If that stability condition is removed, finite variance alone does not even supply a vanishing uniform worst-case expected average-error bound for fixed algorithm parameters.

Theorem 3.8 (Constant worst-case error under bounded variance).

Fix σ,b0,η>0\sigma,b_{0},\eta>0. For every sufficiently large integer TT, there exist a one-dimensional convex 11-smooth function fTf_{T} with fT⋆=0f_{T}^{\star}=0 and an oracle with independent identically distributed additive noise satisfying Assumptions 2 and 4, such that both algorithms, initialized at x1=1x_{1}=1 with x⋆=0x^{\star}=0, satisfy

𝔼⁡[fT​(x¯T)−fT⋆]≥η​σ2256​b02+σ2/16.\mathbb{E}[f_{T}(\bar{x}_{T})-f_{T}^{\star}]\geq\frac{\eta\sigma^{2}}{256\sqrt{b_{0}^{2}+\sigma^{2}/16}}. (3.6)

The objective and noise law may depend on TT, but the initial distance, algorithm parameters, variance bound, and displayed lower-bound constant do not.

Proof sketch.

Use a smooth hinge with slope a=σ/(4​T)a=\sigma/(4\sqrt{T}). In its linear region, the oracle returns −a-a with probability 1−1/T1-1/T; a rare large positive correction preserves unbiasedness and bounded variance. With probability at least 1/41/4, no correction occurs before TT. On that event the accumulator stays bounded, the iterates move away from the minimizer, and their average displacement is of order η​a​T\eta aT. The objective gap is therefore of order η​a2​T\eta a^{2}T, a positive constant in TT. Equations (C.4)–(C.5) in Appendix C make the constants explicit. ∎

Remark 3.9.

This horizon-wise lower bound concerns uniform worst-case convergence, not a failure of convergence on one fixed instance. Unlike the preceding pulse constructions, it uses independent identically distributed additive noise on every fixed instance. The initial distance remains one across the family; the obstruction cannot be attributed to a growing initialization error.

3.4 A logarithmic average-error lower bound under sub-Gaussian noise

The finite-variance counterexamples allow increasingly large gradients. The next construction shows that a loss persists even with uniformly bounded noise. A single scalar, fixed-magnitude oracle proves the result for both algorithms, without an auxiliary coordinate.

Theorem 3.10 (A scalar logarithmic average-error lower bound).

Fix L,σ,b0,η>0L,\sigma,b_{0},\eta>0. For every sufficiently large integer TT, there exist a convex LL-smooth function fT:ℝ→ℝf_{T}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} with fT⋆=0f_{T}^{\star}=0 and an oracle satisfying Assumptions 2 and 3, such that both AdaGrad-Norm and AdaGrad, initialized at x1=x⋆=0x_{1}=x^{\star}=0, satisfy

𝔼⁡[fT​(x¯T)−fT⋆]≥c​η​σ​log⁡TT,\mathbb{E}[f_{T}(\bar{x}_{T})-f_{T}^{\star}]\geq c\eta\sigma\frac{\log T}{\sqrt{T}}, (3.7)

where c>0c>0 is universal. The objective and oracle may depend on TT, but L,σ,b0,ηL,\sigma,b_{0},\eta do not. No horizon-independent bounded-iterate radius is assumed.

Proof sketch.

Choose a smooth hinge with slope a≍σ​log⁡T/Ta\asymp\sigma\sqrt{\log T/T} and an unbiased oracle with gt∈{−γ,γ}g_{t}\in\{-\gamma,\gamma\}, where γ=σ/2\gamma=\sigma/2. Then bt2=b02+t​γ2b_{t}^{2}=b_{0}^{2}+t\gamma^{2} is deterministic. The average splits into a mean-zero martingale term and a nonnegative drift. The squared martingale weights sum to order η2​log⁡T\eta^{2}\log T, so second- and fourth-moment estimates give a positive fluctuation of order η​log⁡T\eta\sqrt{\log T}; see (D.7)–(D.10). Choosing the slope constant small makes the drift smaller than this fluctuation. Multiplication by aa yields (3.7). Appendix D verifies the oracle and smoothing conditions. ∎

Remark 3.11.

The scope of the logarithmic lower bound is smooth-convex average function value, rather than the nonconvex stationarity metric of Jiang et al. [17]. It does not exclude horizon-dependent parameter tuning, alternative outputs, or modifications such as projection. In particular, it does not establish that every logarithm in every AdaGrad upper bound is necessary.

Remark 3.12.

The same construction has a consequence for inverse-square-root SGD: since gt2=γ2g_{t}^{2}=\gamma^{2} on this oracle, AdaGrad is exactly unprojected SGD with deterministic stepsizes η/b02+t​γ2\eta/\sqrt{b_{0}^{2}+t\gamma^{2}}. More generally, fix L,σ,λ,τ>0L,\sigma,\lambda,\tau>0 and consider

xt+1=xt−λt+τ​gt.x_{t+1}=x_{t}-\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{t+\tau}}g_{t}. (3.8)

For every sufficiently large TT, there exists a convex LL-smooth scalar objective fTf_{T}, with x1=x⋆=0x_{1}=x^{\star}=0, for which even the independent additive-noise oracle gt=fT′​(xt)+ξtg_{t}=f_{T}^{\prime}(x_{t})+\xi_{t}, ℙ(ξt=σ/2)=ℙ(ξt=−σ/2)=1/2\mathbb{P}(\xi_{t}=\sigma/2)=\mathbb{P}(\xi_{t}=-\sigma/2)=1/2, satisfies

𝔼⁡[fT​(x¯T)−fT⋆]≥cSGD​λ​σ2​log⁡TT,\mathbb{E}[f_{T}(\bar{x}_{T})-f_{T}^{\star}]\geq c_{\mathrm{SGD}}\lambda\sigma^{2}\frac{\log T}{\sqrt{T}}, (3.9)

where cSGD>0c_{\mathrm{SGD}}>0 is universal. The final part of Appendix D gives the full reduction and checks the independent-noise version. This is a lower bound for a smooth-convex average iterate, not the nonsmooth last-iterate lower bound of Harvey et al. [14]. We are not aware of an earlier result for this exact combination of assumptions and schedule. The qualification on the schedule is essential: the claim does not extend to all SGD stepsizes, suffix averages, or projected variants.

Remark 3.13.

The stepsize schedule matters and cannot be omitted from the statement. For example, for SGD with a constant step 0<α≤1/(2​L)0<\alpha\leq 1/(2L) on a fixed horizon and a conditionally unbiased oracle of variance at most σ2\sigma^{2}, the squared-distance recursion and ‖∇f​(x)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(x)−f⋆)\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\leq 2L(f(x)-f^{\star}) give

𝔼⁡[f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆]≤‖x1−x⋆‖2α​T+α​σ2.\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}]\leq\frac{\|x_{1}-x^{\star}\|^{2}}{\alpha T}+\alpha\sigma^{2}. (3.10)

Indeed, one update decreases expected squared distance by at least α​𝔼​[Δt]−α2​σ2\alpha\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}]-\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}; summation and convexity prove the display. A horizon-dependent choice α≍T−1/2\alpha\asymp T^{-1/2} therefore gives O(T−1/2)O(T^{-1/2}). On the lower-bound instance x1=x⋆x_{1}=x^{\star}, even the initial-distance term vanishes. The logarithm in (3.9) is a limitation of the fixed inverse-square-root schedule with uniform averaging, not of the stochastic oracle problem itself. The final part of Appendix D also verifies the integrability and distance calculation behind (3.10).

3.5 Noise-adaptive upper bounds under the ABC condition

The preceding results distinguish instability, heavy-tail confidence dependence, and last-iterate behavior. None prevents a log-free expected average-error bound under bounded iterates. The final theorem makes this complementary guarantee explicit using the classical regret and self-bounding argument [8, 22, 43, 28].

Theorem 3.14 (Noise-adaptive average-iterate upper bounds).

Under Assumptions 1, 2, and 5, let Q=A+2​L​BQ=A+2LB. For every integer T≥1T\geq 1:

  1. 1.

    AdaGrad-Norm. If ‖xt−x⋆‖≤D\|x_{t}-x^{\star}\|\leq D almost surely for all tt, set Γ=D2/(2​η)+η\Gamma=D^{2}/(2\eta)+\eta. Then

    𝔼⁡[f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆]≤Γ2​Q+Γ​b0T+Γ​CT.\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}]\leq\frac{\Gamma^{2}Q+\Gamma b_{0}}{T}+\Gamma\sqrt{\frac{C}{T}}. (3.11)
  2. 2.

    AdaGrad. If |xt,i−xi⋆|≤Di|x_{t,i}-x_{i}^{\star}|\leq D_{i} almost surely for all t,it,i, set Γi=Di2/(2​η)+η\Gamma_{i}=D_{i}^{2}/(2\eta)+\eta, Λ=(∑iΓi2)1/2\Lambda=(\sum_{i}\Gamma_{i}^{2})^{1/2}, and β0=(∑ib0,i2)1/2\beta_{0}=(\sum_{i}b_{0,i}^{2})^{1/2}. Then

    𝔼⁡[f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆]≤Λ2​Q+Λ​β0T+Λ​CT.\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}]\leq\frac{\Lambda^{2}Q+\Lambda\beta_{0}}{T}+\Lambda\sqrt{\frac{C}{T}}. (3.12)

The radii are nonnegative, finite, and independent of tt. In particular, C=0C=0 gives O⁡(T−1)O(T^{-1}); bounded variance permits Q=2​LQ=2L, C=σ2C=\sigma^{2} and gives O(T−1+σT−1/2)O(T^{-1}+\sigma T^{-1/2}).

Proof sketch.

The key is to retain the objective gap in the second-moment bound instead of replacing it by a uniform constant. For ST=∑t=1T𝔼⁡[Δt]S_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}], smoothness and the ABC condition give ∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖gt‖2]≤Q​ST+C​T\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\|g_{t}\|^{2}]\leq QS_{T}+CT. A pathwise regret inequality removes the correlated denominator before taking expectations, yielding ST≤Γ​b02+Q​ST+C​TS_{T}\leq\Gamma\sqrt{b_{0}^{2}+QS_{T}+CT} for AdaGrad-Norm. For AdaGrad, coordinate-wise regret and Cauchy–Schwarz give the same inequality with (Γ,b0)(\Gamma,b_{0}) replaced by (Λ,β0)(\Lambda,\beta_{0}); see (E.4) and (E.8). Solving these quadratic inequalities produces the noise-adaptive bounds. Appendix E supplies separate proofs for the two algorithms. ∎

Remark 3.15.

Noise adaptation here is conditional on stability, although the algorithms need not know A,B,C,LA,B,C,L or the stability radii. For a common coordinate initialization, β0=d​b0\beta_{0}=\sqrt{d}\,b_{0}. The case C=0C=0 permits state-dependent stochastic noise; it does not require a deterministic oracle. The root-form refinements and the two separate algorithm proofs are in Appendix E. The theorem assumes stability and therefore does not contradict the lower bounds in Sections 3.3 and 3.4, where a common trajectory radius is absent.

4 Conclusion

Our first result rules out any prescribed uniform vanishing expected last-iterate rate for AdaGrad-Norm and AdaGrad under conditional sub-Gaussian oracles, even within an arbitrarily small trajectory radius. One fixed instance violates the proposed rate along a subsequence while still converging; only the pulse schedule depends on that rate.

Under finite variance, a fixed infinite-horizon instance also defeats polynomial average-iterate rates with polylogarithmic confidence dependence within any prescribed radius. A persistent one-sided displacement survives averaging, but the conclusion remains compatible with fixed-confidence convergence and Markov bounds.

Without a common radius, horizon-dependent families give constant worst-case expected average error under finite variance or a logarithmic lower bound under bounded noise. The latter also applies to fixed inverse-square-root SGD, not every stepsize or output. Under bounded iterates, classical regret analysis gives noise-adaptive ABC upper bounds. Identifying sampling assumptions that restore uniform last-iterate rates for the unchanged updates remains an important direction.

APPENDIX

The proofs follow the original order of the main results. Appendix A first proves the absence of a universal last-iterate rate on a fixed instance. Appendix B treats the uniformly averaged output at shrinking confidence levels, still on a fixed infinite-horizon bounded instance. Appendices C and D then construct horizon-dependent expected average-error lower bounds, and the final part of Appendix D proves the SGD consequence. Appendix E provides separate proofs of the two noise-adaptive upper bounds. Each lower-bound construction for AdaGrad is scalar, so the two algorithms have the same trajectory.

Appendix A Proof of Theorem 3.1

We begin with the last-iterate limitation, for which the entire oracle must remain fixed while the evaluation times tend to infinity. The construction below separates the timing of stochastic variation from its magnitude, so a bounded pulse can reveal slow convergence at an arbitrarily late time.

Proof.

The construction starts at the minimizer and keeps the accumulator unchanged until the first nonzero pulse. Choose the objective curvature and pulse size so that a pulse respects the stability radius and every later noise-free update contracts. Specifically, set

ℓ=min⁡{L,b0/(2​η)},d0=min⁡{D/2,η/2},M=b0​d0η2−d02,f⁡(x)=ℓ2​x2.\ell=\min\{L,b_{0}/(2\eta)\},\qquad d_{0}=\min\{D/2,\eta/2\},\qquad M=\frac{b_{0}d_{0}}{\sqrt{\eta^{2}-d_{0}^{2}}},\qquad f(x)=\frac{\ell}{2}x^{2}. (A.1)

Initialize at x1=x⋆=0x_{1}=x^{\star}=0, and let

q=min⁡{14,e−1exp⁡(M2/σ2)−1},qn=q(n+1)2.q=\min\left\{\frac{1}{4},\frac{e-1}{\exp(M^{2}/\sigma^{2})-1}\right\},\qquad q_{n}=\frac{q}{(n+1)^{2}}.

Given a deterministic strictly increasing sequence (τn)n≥1(\tau_{n})_{n\geq 1} of positive integers, allow noise at time t=τnt=\tau_{n} only if no earlier nonzero pulse has occurred. At such an active time, draw ξt=M,−M,0\xi_{t}=M,-M,0 with probabilities qn/2,qn/2,1−qnq_{n}/2,q_{n}/2,1-q_{n}, using fresh randomness. At all other times, including every time after the first nonzero pulse, set ξt=0\xi_{t}=0. Define gt=ℓ​xt+ξtg_{t}=\ell x_{t}+\xi_{t}.

The noise is conditionally symmetric and hence unbiased. At active times,

𝔼⁡[eξt2/σ2∣ℱt−1]=1+qn​(eM2/σ2−1)≤e;\mathbb{E}[e^{\xi_{t}^{2}/\sigma^{2}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=1+q_{n}(e^{M^{2}/\sigma^{2}}-1)\leq e; (A.2)

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 3.5

The preceding proof exploits an accumulator that remains small; we now study the opposite mechanism for the averaged output. A finite cascade increases normalization without leaving a prescribed radius, and the resulting displacement persists long enough to survive uniform averaging.

Proof.

A single sufficiently large gradient can cause a displacement close to η\eta, so it need not respect a prescribed radius D<ηD<\eta. We instead prescribe alternating small displacements and fix their law independently of the eventual evaluation horizons. Let

𝔼⁡[fT​(x¯T)−fT⋆]≥k232​η~​σ​log⁡TT=k264​λ​σ2​log⁡TT.\mathbb{E}[f_{T}(\bar{x}_{T})-f_{T}^{\star}]\geq\frac{k^{2}}{32}\widetilde{\eta}\sigma\frac{\log T}{\sqrt{T}}=\frac{k^{2}}{64}\lambda\sigma^{2}\frac{\log T}{\sqrt{T}}.

The finite-horizon comparison.

For completeness, let SGD use a constant 0<α≤1/(2​L)0<\alpha\leq 1/(2L) and put zt=xt−x⋆z_{t}=x_{t}-x^{\star}. Conditional unbiasedness, convexity, and the smooth self-bound give

𝔼⁡[‖zt+1‖2∣ℱt−1]≤‖zt‖2−2​α​(1−L​α)​Δt+α2​σ2≤‖zt‖2−α​Δt+α2​σ2.\mathbb{E}[\|z_{t+1}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq\|z_{t}\|^{2}-2\alpha(1-L\alpha)\Delta_{t}+\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}\leq\|z_{t}\|^{2}-\alpha\Delta_{t}+\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}.

All finite-time moments here exist: ‖∇f​(xt)‖≤L​‖zt‖\|\nabla f(x_{t})\|\leq L\|z_{t}\| and the variance bound imply, recursively, a finite second moment for ztz_{t} from deterministic x1x_{1}. Taking expectations, summing over t≤Tt\leq T, dropping the nonnegative terminal squared distance, and using convexity of ff proves (3.10). This comparison is a direct distance-recursion calculation, not a claim that every SGD schedule avoids logarithmic losses.

Appendix E Proof of Theorem 3.14

The lower bounds above isolate failures that averaging, tail assumptions, and stability do not individually remove. We now combine expected averaging with bounded iterates and the conditional ABC condition. The proof follows the classical regret and self-bounding approach [8, 22, 43], while retaining the initialization and noise coefficients. After establishing the shared estimates, we give a separate proof for each algorithm.

E.1 Shared self-bounding and integrability estimates

Both proofs close the same quadratic inequality, but use different pathwise regret bounds. We first record the common second-moment estimate and justify the expectations used later. Smoothness applied at x−∇f​(x)/Lx-\nabla f(x)/L gives

f⋆≤f⁡(x−∇f​(x)L)≤f⁡(x)−‖∇f​(x)‖22​L.f^{\star}\leq f\!\left(x-\frac{\nabla f(x)}{L}\right)\leq f(x)-\frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}}{2L}.

Therefore

‖∇f​(x)‖2≤2​L​(f⁡(x)−f⋆).\|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\leq 2L(f(x)-f^{\star}). (E.1)

Writing ST=∑t=1T𝔼⁡[Δt]S_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}] and using Q=A+2​L​BQ=A+2LB, the ABC condition implies

∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖gt‖2]≤Q​ST+C​T.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\|g_{t}\|^{2}]\leq QS_{T}+CT. (E.2)

All terms are finite. Indeed, smoothness at x⋆x^{\star}, where ∇f​(x⋆)=0\nabla f(x^{\star})=0, bounds Δt\Delta_{t} by L​D2/2LD^{2}/2 for AdaGrad-Norm and by (L/2)​∑iDi2(L/2)\sum_{i}D_{i}^{2} for AdaGrad. The ABC condition then gives uniform conditional second-moment bounds. In particular, the accumulators have finite first moments at each finite time, and the inner products with bounded iterates are integrable. These observations justify both the martingale cancellation and the applications of Jensen’s inequality below.

E.2 AdaGrad-Norm

Scalar normalization allows a single Euclidean distance identity. The important order of operations is to sum this identity pathwise before taking expectations, so the correlation between gtg_{t} and btb_{t} never needs to be discarded.

Proof of Theorem 3.14, part 1.

Write zt=xt−x⋆z_{t}=x_{t}-x^{\star}. The actual current-gradient update gives

⟨gt,zt⟩=bt2​η​(‖zt‖2−‖zt+1‖2)+η​‖gt‖22​bt.\langle g_{t},z_{t}\rangle=\frac{b_{t}}{2\eta}(\|z_{t}\|^{2}-\|z_{t+1}\|^{2})+\frac{\eta\|g_{t}\|^{2}}{2b_{t}}.

Summation by parts and ‖zt‖≤D\|z_{t}\|\leq D yield

∑t=1Tbt​(‖zt‖2−‖zt+1‖2)\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t}(\|z_{t}\|^{2}-\|z_{t+1}\|^{2}) =b1​‖z1‖2+∑t=2T(bt−bt−1)​‖zt‖2−bT​‖zT+1‖2\displaystyle=b_{1}\|z_{1}\|^{2}+\sum_{t=2}^{T}(b_{t}-b_{t-1})\|z_{t}\|^{2}-b_{T}\|z_{T+1}\|^{2}
≤D2​bT.\displaystyle\leq D^{2}b_{T}.

Also,

‖gt‖2bt=(bt−bt−1)​(bt+bt−1)bt≤2​(bt−bt−1).\frac{\|g_{t}\|^{2}}{b_{t}}=\frac{(b_{t}-b_{t-1})(b_{t}+b_{t-1})}{b_{t}}\leq 2(b_{t}-b_{t-1}).

Consequently,

∑t=1T⟨gt,zt⟩≤(D22​η+η)​bT−η​b0≤Γ​bT.\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle g_{t},z_{t}\rangle\leq\left(\frac{D^{2}}{2\eta}+\eta\right)b_{T}-\eta b_{0}\leq\Gamma b_{T}. (E.3)

Because ztz_{t} is bounded and ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable, conditional unbiasedness gives 𝔼⁡[⟨ξt,zt⟩]=0\mathbb{E}[\langle\xi_{t},z_{t}\rangle]=0. Convexity and (E.3) thus imply

ST≤∑t=1T𝔼⁡[⟨∇f​(xt),zt⟩]=∑t=1T𝔼⁡[⟨gt,zt⟩]≤Γ​𝔼​[bT].S_{T}\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\langle\nabla f(x_{t}),z_{t}\rangle]=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\langle g_{t},z_{t}\rangle]\leq\Gamma\mathbb{E}[b_{T}].

ST≤Γ​𝔼⁡[bT2]≤Γ​b02+Q​ST+C​T.S_{T}\leq\Gamma\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[b_{T}^{2}]}\leq\Gamma\sqrt{b_{0}^{2}+QS_{T}+CT}. (E.4)

Since ST≥0S_{T}\geq 0, squaring and solving the quadratic inequality yields

ST≤Γ2​Q+Γ4​Q2+4​Γ2​(b02+C​T)2.S_{T}\leq\frac{\Gamma^{2}Q+\sqrt{\Gamma^{4}Q^{2}+4\Gamma^{2}(b_{0}^{2}+CT)}}{2}.

Convexity gives 𝔼⁡[f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆]≤ST/T\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}]\leq S_{T}/T, hence the sharper estimate

𝔼⁡[f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆]≤Γ2​Q+Γ4​Q2+4​Γ2​(b02+C​T)2​T.\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}]\leq\frac{\Gamma^{2}Q+\sqrt{\Gamma^{4}Q^{2}+4\Gamma^{2}(b_{0}^{2}+CT)}}{2T}. (E.5)

Γ4​Q2+4​Γ2​(b02+C​T)≤Γ2​Q+2​Γ​b02+C​T≤Γ2​Q+2​Γ​b0+2​Γ​C​T,\sqrt{\Gamma^{4}Q^{2}+4\Gamma^{2}(b_{0}^{2}+CT)}\leq\Gamma^{2}Q+2\Gamma\sqrt{b_{0}^{2}+CT}\leq\Gamma^{2}Q+2\Gamma b_{0}+2\Gamma\sqrt{CT},

which proves (3.11) with the stated constants. ∎

E.3 Coordinate-wise AdaGrad

Each coordinate has its own accumulator, so one first bounds its scalar regret separately. Summing these bounds and applying Cauchy–Schwarz recovers a scalar quadratic inequality without requiring coordinate-wise ABC assumptions.

Proof of Theorem 3.14, part 2.

Let zt,i=xt,i−xi⋆z_{t,i}=x_{t,i}-x_{i}^{\star}. The update in coordinate ii gives

gt,i​zt,i=bt,i2​η​(zt,i2−zt+1,i2)+η​gt,i22​bt,i.g_{t,i}z_{t,i}=\frac{b_{t,i}}{2\eta}(z_{t,i}^{2}-z_{t+1,i}^{2})+\frac{\eta g_{t,i}^{2}}{2b_{t,i}}.

Since |zt,i|≤Di|z_{t,i}|\leq D_{i} and bt,ib_{t,i} is nondecreasing,

∑t=1Tbt,i​(zt,i2−zt+1,i2)≤Di2​bT,i,∑t=1Tgt,i2bt,i≤2​(bT,i−b0,i).\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}(z_{t,i}^{2}-z_{t+1,i}^{2})\leq D_{i}^{2}b_{T,i},\qquad\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{g_{t,i}^{2}}{b_{t,i}}\leq 2(b_{T,i}-b_{0,i}).

It follows pathwise that

∑t=1Tgt,i​zt,i≤(Di22​η+η)​bT,i−η​b0,i≤Γi​bT,i.\sum_{t=1}^{T}g_{t,i}z_{t,i}\leq\left(\frac{D_{i}^{2}}{2\eta}+\eta\right)b_{T,i}-\eta b_{0,i}\leq\Gamma_{i}b_{T,i}. (E.6)

Summing over ii, taking expectations, and using convexity and conditional unbiasedness after this pathwise estimate gives

ST≤∑i=1dΓi​𝔼​[bT,i]≤∑i=1dΓi​b0,i2+∑t=1T𝔼⁡[gt,i2].S_{T}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Gamma_{i}\mathbb{E}[b_{T,i}]\leq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Gamma_{i}\sqrt{b_{0,i}^{2}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[g_{t,i}^{2}]}. (E.7)

The martingale terms cancel because zt,iz_{t,i} is bounded and ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable. Cauchy–Schwarz and the global estimate (E.2) now yield

ST\displaystyle S_{T} ≤(∑i=1dΓi2)1/2​(∑i=1db0,i2+∑t=1T𝔼⁡[‖gt‖2])1/2\displaystyle\leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Gamma_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}b_{0,i}^{2}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\|g_{t}\|^{2}]\right)^{1/2} (E.8)
≤Λ​β02+Q​ST+C​T.\displaystyle\leq\Lambda\sqrt{\beta_{0}^{2}+QS_{T}+CT}.

Squaring and taking the positive root gives

ST≤Λ2​Q+Λ4​Q2+4​Λ2​(β02+C​T)2.S_{T}\leq\frac{\Lambda^{2}Q+\sqrt{\Lambda^{4}Q^{2}+4\Lambda^{2}(\beta_{0}^{2}+CT)}}{2}.

Dividing by TT and using convexity of ff gives the sharper estimate

𝔼⁡[f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆]≤Λ2​Q+Λ4​Q2+4​Λ2​(β02+C​T)2​T.\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}]\leq\frac{\Lambda^{2}Q+\sqrt{\Lambda^{4}Q^{2}+4\Lambda^{2}(\beta_{0}^{2}+CT)}}{2T}. (E.9)

The estimate

Λ4​Q2+4​Λ2​(β02+C​T)≤Λ2​Q+2​Λ​β0+2​Λ​C​T\sqrt{\Lambda^{4}Q^{2}+4\Lambda^{2}(\beta_{0}^{2}+CT)}\leq\Lambda^{2}Q+2\Lambda\beta_{0}+2\Lambda\sqrt{CT}

then gives (3.12). This argument uses only the global ABC condition. The intermediate bound (E.7) preserves more detailed coordinate-wise second-moment information when it is available. ∎

E.4 Noise specializations and the role of stability

The two proofs have the same final dependence on the residual coefficient CC, even though their geometric constants differ. When C=0C=0, their simplified bounds are (Γ2​Q+Γ​b0)/T(\Gamma^{2}Q+\Gamma b_{0})/T and (Λ2​Q+Λ​β0)/T(\Lambda^{2}Q+\Lambda\beta_{0})/T. This case allows nonzero state-dependent noise; it excludes only an additive residual term in the ABC model.

Under conditional unbiasedness and bounded variance,

𝔼⁡[‖gt‖2∣ℱt−1]=‖∇f​(xt)‖2+𝔼⁡[‖ξt‖2∣ℱt−1]≤‖∇f​(xt)‖2+σ2.\mathbb{E}[\|g_{t}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=\|\nabla f(x_{t})\|^{2}+\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_{t}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq\|\nabla f(x_{t})\|^{2}+\sigma^{2}.

Thus (A,B,C)=(0,1,σ2)(A,B,C)=(0,1,\sigma^{2}), so Q=2​LQ=2L and

𝔼⁡[f⁡(x¯T)−f⋆]≤2​L​Γ2+Γ​b0T+Γ​σT\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{x}_{T})-f^{\star}]\leq\frac{2L\Gamma^{2}+\Gamma b_{0}}{T}+\frac{\Gamma\sigma}{\sqrt{T}}

for AdaGrad-Norm, with the analogous substitution (Γ,b0)↦(Λ,β0)(\Gamma,b_{0})\mapsto(\Lambda,\beta_{0}) for AdaGrad. These guarantees assume a common almost-sure stability radius. They therefore do not contradict the horizon-dependent lower bounds without such a radius, nor do they imply a last-iterate rate or polynomial high-probability bounds with polylogarithmic confidence dependence. Markov’s inequality does give the weaker 1/δ1/\delta dependence in (3.5).
